The physical scale, thermodynamic limit, zero lattice spacing, Euclidean covariance, local spectral content, and non-abelian field geometry must be controlled in one compatible construction. Fix throughout a compact connected simple Lie group G, a faithful unitary representation ρ : G → U (Vρ ) of dimension dρ , and a positive normalization of the invariant quadratic form for which the adjoint color factor is denoted CA (G). The Wilson plaquette function is 1   wG,ρ (U ) = cρ 1 − Re Tr ρ(U ) , dρ where cρ > 0 is chosen once so that the Hessian at the identity is the quadratic form used by the background-field coupling coordinate u = g 2 . This choice is a finite linear normalization of the bare Wilson coupling and is part of the fixed-group input register. Theorem 1.1 (Four-dimensional Yang–Mills construction for fixed compact simple G). For every fixed pair (G, ρ) as above, there is a directed sequence of reflection-positive Wilson lattice measures, with microscopic spacing tending to zero and periodic volume tending to infinity, whose local gauge-invariant curvature-jet Schwinger functions converge to a nontrivial Euclidean field theory on R4 . The limiting Schwinger family is tempered, permutation symmetric, reflection positive, translation continuous, exponentially clustering, and O(4) covariant. Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction yields a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant local theory with a unique vacuum and a number m⋆ (G) > 0 such that H Ω⊥ ≥ m⋆ (G). On the centered invariant weak trajectory, the exact scale-two coupling map is 11 CA (G) log 2 u(2L) = u(L) + u(L)2 + OG (u(L)3 ), 24π 2 with uniform volume and cutoff control in the permanent weak regime. The reconstructed theory contains a nonzero reflected local curvature vector and positive spectral mass in a finite interval [m⋆ (G), M⋆ (G)]. 1.2 Fixed-group conventions and finite register Write g = Lie(G) and dG = dim G. All Haar measures are normalized. The finite-volume approximants use the ordinary periodic link space GE(Λ) with periodic gauge transformations; no twisted boundary condition or nontrivial finite-volume bundle sector is summed. This is sufficient for the claimed local theory on the contractible space R4 . The bi-invariant metric, exponential coordinates, Laplacian ∆G , Casimir eigenvalues, and operator norms are those determined by the declared quadratic form. In curvature formulas, Tr(XY ) denotes this normalized invariant bilinear pairing; raw representation traces are written Tr ρ(·). First, the exact Karcher block is placed in a complete full-alias normal chart and combined with a charged chart-complement partition, permanent analytic domain, marked connected logarithm, Wick-stable jet block, and centered invariant graph. The folded spacetime symbol tensors with Ig , while all nonlinear estimates are admitted by the finite register CG . Second, exact background-scheme conjugacy identifies the universal marginal coefficient and a directed schedule reaches the compact matching scale. The higher product Sobolev operator p (1 − ∆p )sG replaces Q the rank-one order and supplies the fixed-G Fourier–Wiener rows. Third, complete Haar and optical variables are kept in one partition function. A mixed replica– BKAR forest makes every root-to-root path pay separated Haar contraction, optical covariance decay, or pre-existing support charge. Ordinary-periodic toron backgrounds, seams, reflections, and wrapping certificates enter only through the finite template theorem of Appendix D. Finally, a least-label source forest transports the complete invariant-jet system. The degree-four block is group-independent because a compact simple Lie algebra has a unique invariant symmetric bilinear form; possible cubic color tensors first enter the finite dimension-six block. Ward identities, rotation-defect estimates, reflection-positive recombination, and Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction give covariance, the unique vacuum, the gap, and noncollapse. 1.4 External inputs and exact proof boundary Only the theorem-level inputs in Table 1 are imported. The fixed-group geometry, action charge, higher Sobolev landing, periodic-toron template theorem, invariant-jet admission, matching constants, and noncollapse source are internal. There are radii 0 < r0,G < r1,G such that the squared-distance functions, product, inverse, exponential, logarithm, and weighted Karcher critical point extend holomorphically to the corresponding local complexification tube. A compact Lie group with a bi-invariant analytic metric has positive injectivity and strong-convexity radii. The sectional curvature is bounded because G is compact, and the Hessian comparison theorem gives a positive lower Hessian bound on a sufficiently small ball. The analytic implicit-function theorem applied to the Karcher critical equation gives the holomorphic mean. Cauchy estimates on nested compact tubes give every fixed derivative order; standard compact Lie-group analytic facts are summarized in [15]. For a compact simple Lie algebra g: (I1) the invariant symmetric bilinear forms form a one-dimensional space; (I2) there is no reflection-compatible gauge-invariant local vector of engineering dimension at most four; (I3) modulo total differences, equations of motion, and the reflection-odd topological density, the reflection- even scalar dimension-four block is generated by the Yang–Mills density; (I4) the gauge-invariant jet quotient through dimension six is finite. The filtered finite-matrix transport and associated-graded contraction used below therefore apply for every fixed G after enlarging only the finite jet dimension. Proof. Chevalley’s theorem makes the invariant polynomial algebra finitely generated; the degrees are the exponents plus one. Through degree three a primitive symmetric tensor exists only for type Ar , and it first multiplies three curvatures, hence has engineering dimension six. Yang–Mills Existence, Mass Gap, and Nontriviality for Fixed Compact Simple Gauge Groups via Karcher Blocking and Exact Haar–Pivot Matching Harold D. Kirk III1,2,∗ 1 University of Memphis, Memphis, Tennessee 38152, USA 2 ORCID: 0009-0000-6014-8451 August 3, 2026 Abstract Let G be a fixed compact connected simple Lie group and let ρ be a fixed faithful finite-dimensional unitary representation. We construct four-dimensional pure G Yang–Mills theory as a zero-spacing, infinite-volume limit of reflection-positive Wilson lattice measures. The Wilson plaquette function is normalized at the identity to the background quadratic form used to define the coupling u = g 2 . A weighted forty-nine-path Karcher block, complete sixteen-alias normal section, charged chart- complement partition, and permanent rooted domain produce a uniform scale-two map on a centered invariant graph, 11 CA (G) log 2 u(2L) = u(L) + u(L)2 + OG (u(L)3 ). 24π 2 The complete linear block certificate is independent of color and tensors with Ig ; all nonlinear constants are finite and may depend on G. At the physical handoff, a group-dependent product Sobolev order 2sG > dG /2 gives a Peter–Weyl Fourier–Wiener landing for the exact one-pivot and multipivot densities. Separated Haar pivots contract nonvacuum compact flux, optical covariance contracts normal-field stretches, and all remaining vertices retain their support charge. A single marked replica–BKAR forest then gives a boundary-to-center two-root connector and one physical clustering rate. General invariant-jet transport, displacement and stress Ward identities, finite dimension-four mixing, and a dimension-six rotation regulator yield a tempered, reflection-positive, translation-continuous, O(4)-covariant Schwinger family. Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction gives a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant local theory with unique vacuum and a strictly positive Hamiltonian gap. Endpoint-safe curvature-source transport produces a nonzero local vector with positive spectral mass in a finite interval above the gap. The theorem concerns the local gauge-invariant curvature-jet observable theory. No estimate is asserted uniformly over the class of compact simple groups. ∗ hkirk@memphis.edu 1 Contents 1 The compact-simple-group theorem and proof boundary 3 2 Fixed-group Wilson geometry and Karcher blocking 5 3 Charged chart complement and irregular sector 10 4 Permanent weak renormalization group 23 5 Invariant graph and universal coefficient 39 6 Directed handoff and higher-order Peter–Weyl landing 52 7 Compact boundary-to-center closure 71 8 General invariant jets and Ward identities 72 9 Continuum reconstruction and spectral gap 89 10 Nontriviality and finite spectral window 90 11 Completion for arbitrary fixed compact simple gauge groups 94 A Endpoint packet-shell verification 94 B Root data and representation normalization 109 C The fixed-group Sobolev and Peter–Weyl ledger 110 D Ordinary periodic torons, seams, and wrapping templates 110 E Invariant tensor spaces through engineering dimension six 111 F Theorem-level specialization and dependency map 112 G Representative fixed-group certifications 113 2 1 The compact-simple-group theorem and proof boundary 1.1 Problem and result The constructive Yang–Mills problem asks for a nontrivial quantum gauge field theory on R4 satisfying the Osterwalder–Schrader and Wightman requirements and possessing a strictly positive mass gap [1]. The physical scale, thermodynamic limit, zero lattice spacing, Euclidean covariance, local spectral content, and non-abelian field geometry must be controlled in one compatible construction. Fix throughout a compact connected simple Lie group G, a faithful unitary representation ρ : G → U (Vρ ) of dimension dρ , and a positive normalization of the invariant quadratic form for which the adjoint color factor is denoted CA (G). The Wilson plaquette function is 1   wG,ρ (U ) = cρ 1 − Re Tr ρ(U ) , dρ where cρ > 0 is chosen once so that the Hessian at the identity is the quadratic form used by the background-field coupling coordinate u = g 2 . This choice is a finite linear normalization of the bare Wilson coupling and is part of the fixed-group input register. Theorem 1.1 (Four-dimensional Yang–Mills construction for fixed compact simple G). For every fixed pair (G, ρ) as above, there is a directed sequence of reflection-positive Wilson lattice measures, with microscopic spacing tending to zero and periodic volume tending to infinity, whose local gauge-invariant curvature-jet Schwinger functions converge to a nontrivial Euclidean field theory on R4 . The limiting Schwinger family is tempered, permutation symmetric, reflection positive, translation continuous, exponentially clustering, and O(4) covariant. Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction yields a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant local theory with a unique vacuum and a number m⋆ (G) > 0 such that H Ω⊥ ≥ m⋆ (G). On the centered invariant weak trajectory, the exact scale-two coupling map is 11 CA (G) log 2 u(2L) = u(L) + u(L)2 + OG (u(L)3 ), 24π 2 with uniform volume and cutoff control in the permanent weak regime. The reconstructed theory contains a nonzero reflected local curvature vector and positive spectral mass in a finite interval [m⋆ (G), M⋆ (G)]. 1.2 Fixed-group conventions and finite register Write g = Lie(G) and dG = dim G. All Haar measures are normalized. In curvature formulas, Tr(XY ) denotes this normalized invariant bilinear pairing; raw representation traces are written Tr ρ(·). First, the exact Karcher block is placed in a complete full-alias normal chart and combined with a charged chart-complement partition, permanent analytic domain, marked connected logarithm, Wick-stable jet block, and centered invariant graph. The folded spacetime symbol tensors with Ig , while all nonlinear estimates are admitted by the finite register CG . Second, exact background-scheme conjugacy identifies the universal marginal coefficient and a directed schedule reaches the compact matching scale. Ordinary-periodic toron backgrounds, seams, reflections, and wrapping certificates enter only through the finite template theorem of Appendix D. Finally, a least-label source forest transports the complete invariant-jet system. The degree-four block is group-independent because a compact simple Lie algebra has a unique invariant symmetric bilinear form; possible cubic color tensors first enter the finite dimension-six block. The sectional curvature is bounded because G is compact, and the Hessian comparison theorem gives a positive lower Hessian bound on a sufficiently small ball. D Ordinary periodic torons, seams, and wrapping templates The finite-volume model used throughout is the ordinary periodic product space GE(Λ) with periodic gauge transformations. It is a single, explicit lattice model; no twisted boundary condition and no sum over nontrivial principal-bundle sectors is part of the construction. Since the target spacetime R4 is contractible, this restriction is compatible with the theorem’s local continuum scope. Define the compact set of ordinary periodic flat holonomies TG := {(h1 , h2 , h3 , h4 ) ∈ G4 : [hµ , hν ] = e for all µ, ν}. Lemma D.1 (Tree-gauge reduction of ordinary periodic flat fields). Every flat configuration in the ordinary periodic link model is gauge equivalent to a seam representative whose interior links are the identity and whose four fundamental seam holonomies form an element of TG . Conversely every element of TG defines such a flat periodic configuration. The remaining gauge action is simultaneous conjugation of the four holonomies. 110 Proof. Choose a maximal lattice tree in a fundamental periodic cell and gauge its links to the identity. Flatness makes the holonomy of a path depend only on its homotopy class. The four links closing the fundamental cycles therefore supply holonomies hµ . The commutator loop of two fundamental cycles is a product of plaquette boundaries, so flatness gives [hµ , hν ] = e. Reversing this construction gives a flat seam representative from every commuting four-tuple. A gauge transformation at the tree root conjugates all four holonomies simultaneously, and all other gauge freedom has already been fixed. Lemma D.2 (Finite toron and seam atlas). For every fixed compact G, the set TG has a finite cover by ambient product-coordinate neighborhoods on which every block word, Karcher word, coarea factor, Haar factor, reflected word, and source word used in the proof is analytic in the local variables and in the toron parameters. All derivatives through order 2sG + 3 have a finite common bound. The aligned coordinate reflections and seam placements add only a finite template family. Proof. The commutator equations define a closed subset of compact G4 , hence TG is compact. Around each of its points choose ordinary product charts in the ambient manifold G4 ; no quotient chart or classification of singular conjugacy classes is required. In tree gauge, every local factor is a fixed finite composition of multiplication, inversion, the local exponential/logarithm, and the Karcher implicit function, with some arguments left- or right-multiplied by the fixed seam holonomies. These maps are analytic on a sufficiently small product neighborhood and have finite Cauchy bounds through the declared order. Compactness gives a finite subcover. There are four seam directions and a finite aligned-reflection family, so taking a finite maximum gives the common constants. Theorem D.3 (Ordinary-periodic toron and optical admission). The complete full-alias right-inverse, normal-section, optical-coercivity, Haar-minorization, owner, and boundary-to-center estimates hold uniformly over every flat toron background in TG , every admitted seam and aligned-reflection template, and every periodic wrapping certificate. The acoustic toron/background variables remain explicit and are never inverted. No constant uniform over different groups is asserted. Proof. Lift a seam representative to the universal covering lattice. A flat background is gauged to the identity there; deck translation in direction µ acts on Lie-algebra fields by the unitary operator Ad(hµ ). Since the hµ commute, these unitary operators are simultaneously diagonalizable over the complexified color space. On each joint color eigenspace the folded block and optical symbols are therefore the identity-background, color-free symbols evaluated at a real quasi-momentum shifted by the corresponding deck phase. The estimates 49 8 Af (k)Af (k)∗ ⪰ I4 , ∥P0 (k)∥2 ≤ , 2 49 and the printed complex-strip and optical lower bounds hold for every real quasi-momentum. They consequently survive every toron phase without a loss of constant. The retained acoustic variables, including toron tangents, are kept in the exterior/background register; only the same normal optical complement is inverted. Lemma D.2 supplies the nonlinear, coarea, Haar, and marked derivative bounds uniformly over a finite toron/seam cover. On the covering lattice the local gauge trivialization sends every plaquette holonomy to a conjugate of the corresponding fluctuation plaquette. The representation-normalized Wilson function is conjugation invariant, so the charge and its differentiated finite-word ledger are unchanged by this trivialization. The 2sG differentiated bad-core row of Theorem 3.20 is therefore uniform on the same cover. Consequently the complete one-pivot score and Haar minorization retain their printed constants after taking the finite template maximum. On intersections use the fixed least-label owner, so no factor is duplicated. A wrapping certificate records only the four lattice directions, the fixed block range, a finite seam crossing pattern, and an aligned reflection type; there are finitely many such local templates at one normalized step. Their iteration is already controlled by the permanent wrapping ideal rather than by a sum over topological sectors. Taking the finite maximum proves the stated admission and leaves the joint Haar–optical boundary-to-center mechanism unchanged. A source derivative is a labelled leaf. At one conditional integration, connected cumulant differentiation joins a nonempty partition of the incoming leaves and decorated subtrees to one new vertex labelled by that integration scale. Fix an engineering cutoff D. Proof. After a boundary-rooted tree gauge, one enlarged block cell contains a finite alphabet of Lie-algebra variables and difference labels. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF , hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). Theorem 8.46 (Euclidean covariance and Poincaré reconstruction). The Schwinger family satisfies the full O(4) covariance axiom. Together with reflection positivity, permutation symmetry, temperedness and continuous translations, this gives by the Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction theorem a strongly continuous unitary representation of the proper orthochronous Poincaré group on the reconstructed Hilbert space, with translation spectrum in the closed forward cone. The multiscale source-tree theorem supplies a projective Schwinger functional S on D with the following properties: (S1) temperedness and continuity in every Schwartz test tensor; (S2) stationarity, gauge invariance, permutation symmetry, and reflection positivity; (S3) continuous Euclidean translations; (S4) for every two field polynomials F, G with separated supports, |S(F G) − S(F )S(G)| ≤ CF,G e−m dist1 (supp F,supp G) (166) with one m > 0 independent of the chosen polynomials; (S5) the OS linear-growth estimate of Lemma 8.13 on every finite source multiplet. The constants CF,G may depend on the fixed fields and test functions; the exponent m does not. Theorem 9.1 (Continuous OS reconstruction). Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T (t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection positivity gives the positive form and the null ideal N = {F : ∥F ∥OS = 0}. Positive-time translations preserve D+ for sufficiently small translations on each compactly supported word and define contractions on the quotient; the usual time-zero limiting argument extends them to all t ≥ 0. For a core vector [F ], 2 ∥T (t)[F ] − [F ]∥ = S(ΘF τ2t F ) − 2ℜS(ΘF τt F ) + S(ΘF F ), which tends to zero by translation continuity. Contractivity and density give strong continuity on H. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T (t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν ) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF ) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F ) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(Fµα Fνα ), δµν Tr F 2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. The first is symmetric; the dual contraction is proportional to a diagonal pseudoscalar tensor; none has an antisymmetric part. Reflection symmetry excludes the odd-derivative dimension-five sector. Corollary 8.40 (Vanishing rotation regulator). In the projective stress Ward identity, the antisymmetric regulator insertion is a2 times a normalized family of dimension-six roots. The marked source bounds therefore make it vanish in the zero-spacing limit. The cutoff rotation Ward identities integrate to full O(4) covariance once the already established translation, reflection, and tensor-source continuity statements are inserted. The multiscale source-tree theorem supplies a projective Schwinger functional S on D with the following properties: (S1) temperedness and continuity in every Schwartz test tensor; (S2) stationarity, gauge invariance, permutation symmetry, and reflection positivity; (S3) continuous Euclidean translations; (S4) for every two field polynomials F, G with separated supports, |S(F G) − S(F )S(G)| ≤ CF,G e−m dist1 (supp F,supp G) (166) with one m > 0 independent of the chosen polynomials; (S5) the OS linear-growth estimate of Lemma 8.13 on every finite source multiplet. The constants CF,G may depend on the fixed fields and test functions; the exponent m does not. Theorem 9.1 (Continuous OS reconstruction). Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T (t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection positivity gives the positive form and the null ideal N = {F : ∥F ∥OS = 0}. Positive-time translations preserve D+ for sufficiently small translations on each compactly supported word and define contractions on the quotient; the usual time-zero limiting argument extends them to all t ≥ 0. For a core vector [F ], 2 ∥T (t)[F ] − [F ]∥ = S(ΘF τ2t F ) − 2ℜS(ΘF τt F ) + S(ΘF F ), which tends to zero by translation continuity. Contractivity and density give strong continuity on H. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T (t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. Multiplication by e(m−ε)t and t → ∞ gives µF ([0, m − ε]) = 0. Letting ε ↓ 0 proves (167). Theorem 9.3 (Unique vacuum and complete local mass gap). The OS Hamiltonian satisfies H Ω⊥ ≥ m > 0. (169) The vacuum is unique. Proof. The centered classes [F ] − S(F )Ω, F ∈ D+ , are dense in Ω⊥ . Lemma 9.2 says that the spectral projection EH ([0, m − ε]) annihilates this dense set for every ε > 0; hence it vanishes on Ω⊥ . This proves the absence of spectrum in (0, m). For a centered core vector, (168) tends to zero, so its spectral measure has no atom at zero. Density then shows that EH ({0})H = CΩ. Thus the vacuum is unique and (169) holds. 10 Nontriviality and finite spectral window 10.1 Endpoint interpolation and reflected noncollapse Let Yr (f ) be the tangent-normalized, Wick-centered scalar curvature source at physical scale r, with the source root parallel transported in the normalized finite-jet frame. Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν ) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF ) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F ) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(Fµα Fνα ), δµν Tr F 2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. The first is symmetric; the dual contraction is proportional to a diagonal pseudoscalar tensor; none has an antisymmetric part. Reflection symmetry excludes the odd-derivative dimension-five sector. Finite source multiplets and integration For every D < ∞, let J≤D be the finite-dimensional renormalized curvature-jet source multiplet. The contact hierarchy preserves the engineering filtration. Theorem 8.46 (Euclidean covariance and Poincaré reconstruction). The Schwinger family satisfies the full O(4) covariance axiom. Together with reflection positivity, permutation symmetry, temperedness and continuous translations, this gives by the Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction theorem a strongly continuous unitary representation of the proper orthochronous Poincaré group on the reconstructed Hilbert space, with translation spectrum in the closed forward cone. The standard Osterwalder–Schrader covariance reconstruction then produces the positive- energy Poincaré representation. The multiscale source-tree theorem supplies a projective Schwinger functional S on D with the following properties: (S1) temperedness and continuity in every Schwartz test tensor; (S2) stationarity, gauge invariance, permutation symmetry, and reflection positivity; (S3) continuous Euclidean translations; (S4) for every two field polynomials F, G with separated supports, |S(F G) − S(F )S(G)| ≤ CF,G e−m dist1 (supp F,supp G) (166) with one m > 0 independent of the chosen polynomials; (S5) the OS linear-growth estimate of Lemma 8.13 on every finite source multiplet. The constants CF,G may depend on the fixed fields and test functions; the exponent m does not. Theorem 9.1 (Continuous OS reconstruction). Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T (t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection positivity gives the positive form and the null ideal N = {F : ∥F ∥OS = 0}. Positive-time translations preserve D+ for sufficiently small translations on each compactly supported word and define contractions on the quotient; the usual time-zero limiting argument extends them to all t ≥ 0. For a core vector [F ], 2 ∥T (t)[F ] − [F ]∥ = S(ΘF τ2t F ) − 2ℜS(ΘF τt F ) + S(ΘF F ), which tends to zero by translation continuity. Contractivity and density give strong continuity on H. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T (t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. Spectral consequence of one common clustering rate Let D+,0 be the centered positive-time core, D+,0 = {F ∈ D+ : S(F ) = 0}. For F ∈ D+,0 let µF be the positive spectral measure of H in the vector [F ]. 89 Lemma 9.2 (Core spectral support). For every F ∈ D+,0 , supp µF ⊂ [m, ∞). (167) Proof. Let the time support of F lie in a fixed compact interval. For all sufficiently large t, the supports of ΘF and τt F are separated by at least t − cF . Since S(F ) = 0, (166) and OS reconstruction give Z ∞ 0≤ e−tλ dµF (λ) = ⟨[F ], T (t)[F ]⟩ ≤ CF e−mt . (168) 0 Fix ε > 0. Then e−(m−ε)t µF ([0, m − ε]) ≤ CF e−mt . Multiplication by e(m−ε)t and t → ∞ gives µF ([0, m − ε]) = 0. Letting ε ↓ 0 proves (167). Theorem 9.3 (Unique vacuum and complete local mass gap). The OS Hamiltonian satisfies H Ω⊥ ≥ m > 0. (169) The vacuum is unique. Proof. The centered classes [F ] − S(F )Ω, F ∈ D+ , are dense in Ω⊥ . Lemma 9.2 says that the spectral projection EH ([0, m − ε]) annihilates this dense set for every ε > 0; hence it vanishes on Ω⊥ . This proves the absence of spectrum in (0, m). For a centered core vector, (168) tends to zero, so its spectral measure has no atom at zero. Density then shows that EH ({0})H = CΩ. Thus the vacuum is unique and (169) holds. 10 Nontriviality and finite spectral window 10.1 Endpoint interpolation and reflected noncollapse Let Yr (f ) be the tangent-normalized, Wick-centered scalar curvature source at physical scale r, with the source root parallel transported in the normalized finite-jet frame. Fix an engineering cutoff D. Modulo vacuum constants, total lattice differences, gauge and Bianchi identities, equation-of-motion/redundant directions, and the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills coordinate, the local gauge-invariant curvature jets of dimension at most D form a finite graded space M J≤D = J∆ . ∆≤D The same remains true after adjoining any fixed finite collection of retained, source, displacement, profile, stress, rotation-defect, and one/two-root marks. Proof. After a boundary-rooted tree gauge, one enlarged block cell contains a finite alphabet of Lie-algebra variables and difference labels. Jets of bounded engineering dimension form a finite polynomial span. Every listed quotient relation is linear on that span, and adjoining finitely many marks gives a finite direct sum. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF , hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). Theorem 5.18 (Compact weakening). If a > 0, a′ > 0, and a′ < a, every bounded subset of Ba,N , N ≥ 1, is relatively compact in Ba′ ,N −1 . Proof. Let F be bounded by M in Ba,N . For a cutoff L, X ′ ′ sup ea |X| ∥FX ∥C N −1 ≤ e−(a−a )L M, e X∋e |X|>L uniformly in F ∈ F. For |X| ≤ L, only finitely many rooted support shapes occur. On each shape, the C N (KX ) bound is uniform, and the compact embedding C N (KX ) ⋐ C N −1 (KX ) follows from Arzela–Ascoli in finitely many coordinate charts. A diagonal subsequence converges on all shapes of size at most L. Letting L increase and using the uniform tail estimate proves relative compactness in Ba′ ,N −1 . Theorem 5.19 (Exact fiber-chart invariance). Let Ψ1 (w, z1 ) and Ψ2 (w, z2 ) be two exact C 1 fiber charts for the same finite-dimensional submersion B(U ) = w. Suppose their images agree on the integration region and their transition map is orientation preserving. Then, for every integrable density F , Z Z F (Ψ1 (w, z1 )) J1 (w, z1 ) dz1 = F (Ψ2 (w, z2 )) J2 (w, z2 ) dz2 . Consequently the normalized conditional expectation, its connected logarithm, and every background derivative of the complete local standard-scheme coordinate and its quadratic coefficient are independent of the chosen exact fiber chart. 48 Proof. The first identity is the ordinary change-of-variables theorem on the fiber. Division by the same fiber mass gives equality of normalized conditional expectations. Connected logarithms are functions of those expectations. Differentiation is permitted on any common dominated marked domain. The determinant statement follows because the two Jacobians are related by the determinant of the transition map, which cancels under the change of variables. It must not be inserted a second time. 5.4 Ultraviolet supplier closure The finite-volume normal chart, strict macrostep contraction, and irregular Fréchet flatness used below are not separate inputs: they are respectively Theorem 2.5, Theorem 4.30, and Theorem 3.31. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF , hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF , hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). A source derivative is a labelled leaf. At one conditional integration, connected cumulant differentiation joins a nonempty partition of the incoming leaves and decorated subtrees to one new vertex labelled by that integration scale. Terms transported without joining retain their existing components. At the terminal matching logarithm, the remaining components are joined by the matching-scale connected cumulants. The ordering of children is fixed by the least source label, so isomorphic terms are not counted more than once. Lemma 8.6 (Exact multiscale Faà di Bruno forest formula). Lemma 8.10 (Labelled-tree extraction). Every connected source-labelled history admits a deterministic allocation to a spanning tree on {1, . . . , n}. For a compact simple Lie algebra g: (I1) the invariant symmetric bilinear forms form a one-dimensional space; (I2) there is no reflection-compatible gauge-invariant local vector of engineering dimension at most four; (I3) modulo total differences, equations of motion, and the reflection-odd topological density, the reflection- even scalar dimension-four block is generated by the Yang–Mills density; (I4) the gauge-invariant jet quotient through dimension six is finite. A primitive cubic symmetric color tensor occurs precisely for Lie type Ar with r ≥ 2 and is retained in the dimension-six block; its presence does not enlarge the dimension-four marginal block. The filtered finite-matrix transport and associated-graded contraction used below therefore apply for every fixed G after enlarging only the finite jet dimension. Proof. Simplicity gives the uniqueness of the invariant bilinear form. Semisimplicity makes every finite- dimensional representation traceless on g. Lorentz index counting, gauge covariance, and reflection parity then exclude a single free vector index through dimension four and leave only the quadratic curvature scalar in the even dimension-four sector. Chevalley’s theorem makes the invariant polynomial algebra finitely generated; the degrees are the exponents plus one. Through degree three a primitive symmetric tensor exists only for type Ar , and it first multiplies three curvatures, hence has engineering dimension six. The multiscale source-tree theorem supplies a projective Schwinger functional S on D with the following properties: (S1) temperedness and continuity in every Schwartz test tensor; (S2) stationarity, gauge invariance, permutation symmetry, and reflection positivity; (S3) continuous Euclidean translations; (S4) for every two field polynomials F, G with separated supports, |S(F G) − S(F )S(G)| ≤ CF,G e−m dist1 (supp F,supp G) (166) with one m > 0 independent of the chosen polynomials; (S5) the OS linear-growth estimate of Lemma 8.13 on every finite source multiplet. The constants CF,G may depend on the fixed fields and test functions; the exponent m does not. Theorem 9.1 (Continuous OS reconstruction). Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T (t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection positivity gives the positive form and the null ideal N = {F : ∥F ∥OS = 0}. Positive-time translations preserve D+ for sufficiently small translations on each compactly supported word and define contractions on the quotient; the usual time-zero limiting argument extends them to all t ≥ 0. For a core vector [F ], 2 ∥T (t)[F ] − [F ]∥ = S(ΘF τ2t F ) − 2ℜS(ΘF τt F ) + S(ΘF F ), which tends to zero by translation continuity. Contractivity and density give strong continuity on H. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T (t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. lassification. Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν ) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF ) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F ) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(Fµα Fνα ), δµν Tr F 2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. The first is symmetric; the dual contraction is proportional to a diagonal pseudoscalar tensor; none has an antisymmetric part. Reflection symmetry excludes the odd-derivative dimension-five sector. Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T (t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T (t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. Finite source multiplets and integration For every D < ∞, let J≤D be the finite-dimensional renormalized curvature-jet source multiplet. The contact hierarchy preserves the engineering filtration. On J≤D , δω is a finite matrix, allowing same-dimension composite-operator mixing. Lemma 8.44 (Rotation algebra on finite source multiplets). The contact derivations obey [δω , δη ] = δ[ω,η] on every J≤D and are compatible under D 7→ D + 2. Proof. At finite cutoff the contact derivations are obtained by differentiating the geometric pullback of test profiles, tensor indices and local source words. Geometric Lie derivatives obey the displayed commutator identity exactly. Finite triangular source renormalization conjugates this finite-dimensional action and therefore preserves the commutator. Dimension-raised regulator contacts vanish by Lemma 8.41; the projective limit and the inclusions of source multiplets preserve the identity. Every finite-dimensional real representation of so(4) integrates to the simply connected group Spin(4). The source multiplets consist of bosonic tensors built from curvature and covariant derivatives, so a 2π rotation acts trivially; equivalently, their geometric tensor action factors through SO(4). Theorem 8.45 (SO(4) covariance of the Schwinger family). Let ρD be the integrated finite-dimensional action on J≤D . Then for every R ∈ SO(4), Sn (ρD (R)v1 , Rf1 ), . . . , (ρD (R)vn , Rfn )  = Sn (v1 , f1 ), . . . , (vn , fn ) .  Exact lattice reflection extends the covariance to O(4). Proof. Along a smooth path R(s) in SO(4), differentiate the transformed Schwinger function. The derivative is the left side of (165) with ω = R′ (s)R(s)−1 and therefore vanishes. Lemma 8.44 gives path independence and the group law. Reflection is exact for the Wilson action, block map, clover source and finite source normalization. 88 Osterwalder–Schrader continuation Let Dloc be the local field-polynomial test algebra. The O(4) covariance proved above is an identity of the Euclidean Schwinger system. Rotations preserving the chosen time-zero hyperplane act directly on the positive-time quotient; rotations mixing Euclidean time with space need not preserve that quotient and are not asserted to act unitarily there. Theorem 8.46 (Euclidean covariance and Poincaré reconstruction). The Schwinger family satisfies the full O(4) covariance axiom. Together with reflection positivity, permutation symmetry, temperedness and continuous translations, this gives by the Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction theorem a strongly continuous unitary representation of the proper orthochronous Poincaré group on the reconstructed Hilbert space, with translation spectrum in the closed forward cone. Spatial rotations and translations are obtained directly on the OS quotient; Lorentz boosts arise from analytic continuation of the Euclidean rotation covariance. Proof. Theorem 8.45 is precisely the Euclidean covariance identity required for every finite tensor/source multiplet, and the nested source construction extends it to the complete chosen local field family. The direct OS theorem, Lemma 8.14, and Lemma 8.13 supply the remaining reconstruction hypotheses, including the linear-growth condition. The standard Osterwalder–Schrader covariance reconstruction then produces the positive- energy Poincaré representation. No unitary action of a Euclidean rotation that changes the reflection hyperplane is assumed on the intermediate OS quotient. 9 Continuum reconstruction and spectral gap 9.1 Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction and clustering gap The common Schwinger functional Let D be the countable algebra generated by positive-time translates of the bounded positive-scale cylinders and the normalized finite local source fields constructed by the marked hierarchy. The multiscale source-tree theorem supplies a projective Schwinger functional S on D with the following properties: (S1) temperedness and continuity in every Schwartz test tensor; (S2) stationarity, gauge invariance, permutation symmetry, and reflection positivity; (S3) continuous Euclidean translations; (S4) for every two field polynomials F, G with separated supports, |S(F G) − S(F )S(G)| ≤ CF,G e−m dist1 (supp F,supp G) (166) with one m > 0 independent of the chosen polynomials; (S5) the OS linear-growth estimate of Lemma 8.13 on every finite source multiplet. The constants CF,G may depend on the fixed fields and test functions; the exponent m does not. Theorem 9.1 (Continuous OS reconstruction). Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T (t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection positivity gives the positive form and the null ideal N = {F : ∥F ∥OS = 0}. Positive-time translations preserve D+ for sufficiently small translations on each compactly supported word and define contractions on the quotient; the usual time-zero limiting argument extends them to all t ≥ 0. For a core vector [F ], 2 ∥T (t)[F ] − [F ]∥ = S(ΘF τ2t F ) − 2ℜS(ΘF τt F ) + S(ΘF F ), which tends to zero by translation continuity. Contractivity and density give strong continuity on H. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T (t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. Spectral consequence of one common clustering rate Let D+,0 be the centered positive-time core, D+,0 = {F ∈ D+ : S(F ) = 0}. For F ∈ D+,0 let µF be the positive spectral measure of H in the vector [F ]. 89 Lemma 9.2 (Core spectral support). For every F ∈ D+,0 , supp µF ⊂ [m, ∞). (167) Proof. Let the time support of F lie in a fixed compact interval. For all sufficiently large t, the supports of ΘF and τt F are separated by at least t − cF . Since S(F ) = 0, (166) and OS reconstruction give Z ∞ 0≤ e−tλ dµF (λ) = ⟨[F ], T (t)[F ]⟩ ≤ CF e−mt . (168) 0 Fix ε > 0. Then e−(m−ε)t µF ([0, m − ε]) ≤ CF e−mt . Multiplication by e(m−ε)t and t → ∞ gives µF ([0, m − ε]) = 0. Letting ε ↓ 0 proves (167). Theorem 9.3 (Unique vacuum and complete local mass gap). The OS Hamiltonian satisfies H Ω⊥ ≥ m > 0. (169) The vacuum is unique. Proof. The centered classes [F ] − S(F )Ω, F ∈ D+ , are dense in Ω⊥ . Lemma 9.2 says that the spectral projection EH ([0, m − ε]) annihilates this dense set for every ε > 0; hence it vanishes on Ω⊥ . This proves the absence of spectrum in (0, m). For a centered core vector, (168) tends to zero, so its spectral measure has no atom at zero. Density then shows that EH ({0})H = CΩ. Thus the vacuum is unique and (169) holds. 10 Nontriviality and finite spectral window 10.1 Endpoint interpolation and reflected noncollapse Let Yr (f ) be the tangent-normalized, Wick-centered scalar curvature source at physical scale r, with the source root parallel transported in the normalized finite-jet frame.
